newsitem.title: USA: U.S. researchers identify new Alzheimer's feature.
newsitem.headline: U.S. researchers identify new Alzheimer's feature.

text.p: Researchers identified a previously unknown way that Alzheimer's disease physically affects the brain, according to a study released on Thursday.

The study, in the July issue of the American Journal of Pathology, found that the disease creates a plaquelike lesion that can account for up to one-third of the damage, by volume, caused by Alzheimer's in the brains of afflicted patients.
The lesions are rare or absent in other degenerative brain diseases, which means they could provide new clues to the development and possible treatment of the disease.

"This is a spectacular lesion, never before seen, that tracks closely with the disease state," Dr. John Trojanowski, a University of Pennsylvania medical professor and senior author of the study report, said.
"We have every reason to suspect that this pathology will be found to play a crucial role in the development and progression of Alzheimer's disease," he said in a statement.

Alzheimer's affects about 15 percent of people over age 65 and about half those over 85. It often begins with memory loss and progresses to severe dementia and death. Former President Ronald Reagan suffers from the disease.

Previously, the disease was known to cause tangled fibers aligned with nerve cells in the brain and what is called "amyloid plaque." The new lesions -- the third way the disease physically affects the brain -- were found using antibodies that revealed their existence.
Earlier staining and dyeing methods used for analyzing the brains of Alzhemier's patients failed to detect the lesions.
Zaven Khachaturian, director of the Alzheimer's Association's Ronald and Nancy Reagan Research Institute, called the study "potentially a very significant finding."

"This discovery may open fresh avenues for investigating the cause or causes of Alzheimer's, give us a new diagnostic marker and provide new targets for treatments," he said in the University of Pennsylvania press release.
